title: The African Elephant
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The African elephant is the largest animal that lives on land. A fully grown bull can stand three and a half metres at the shoulder and weigh up to six tonnes, as much as five or six family cars. Despite its size, the elephant is gentle and highly intelligent, with a brain that is the biggest of any land animal, and its social life is as complex as that of any creature except humans. For these reasons elephants have fascinated people for thousands of years, and they have appeared in the myths, art and wars of many cultures. This passage describes their remarkable bodies and minds and the dangers they now face.

The trunk is the elephant's most useful tool. It is a combination of the nose and the upper lip, and it contains about forty thousand separate muscles, but no bones. With it, an elephant can lift a log weighing several hundred kilograms or pick up a single peanut. It is used for breathing, smelling, drinking, which means sucking up as much as ten litres of water and squirting it into the mouth, and for greeting other elephants by touch. The elephant can also use the trunk as a snorkel when it crosses deep rivers. The tusks, which are very long teeth, are used for digging, for stripping bark from trees and for defence.

Elephants live in family groups, led by the oldest female, the matriarch. A herd usually consists of her sisters, daughters and their young, perhaps ten or twenty animals in all. The matriarch's most valuable asset is her memory: she remembers where to find water in a drought, which routes are safe, and which other herds are friends or enemies. Young males leave the herd at about fourteen years old and live alone or with other males. Calves are born after a pregnancy of twenty-two months, the longest of any mammal, and the whole herd helps to protect and raise them.

Elephants communicate in many ways. They trumpet when excited or alarmed, and they use a range of rumbles, snorts and cries. Some of the rumbles are so low that humans cannot hear them; these sounds, called infrasound, travel for kilometres through the ground and the air, so that herds that cannot see one another can still keep in contact. Elephants can feel these vibrations through the soles of their feet, and they sometimes stand still with one foot raised, apparently listening. They also have a range of body language, flapping their ears, raising their trunks or touching one another gently when they meet.

Elephants show signs of intelligence and emotion that few other animals match. Like dolphins and apes, they can recognise themselves in a mirror, a test which only a small number of species pass. They use tools, breaking branches to swat flies, and they have been seen to help injured companions. A herd will gather around a dead relative, touch the bones with their trunks and stay for hours, behaviour which suggests grief. Researchers have also recorded elephants showing great concern for the young, comforting a calf which is frightened with a gentle touch of the trunk.

Sadly, elephants are in danger. A century ago there were several million African elephants; today there are fewer than half a million. The main threat is the loss of habitat: as human populations grow, farms and roads divide the land, and elephants that wander on to fields may destroy a family's harvest in a single night. The second is poaching for ivory, which has killed tens of thousands of animals in some years. Because elephants live for up to seventy years and breed slowly, a population needs decades to recover from heavy losses.

Dr Wanjiru Kamau, a conservation biologist in Kenya, leads a project that helps farmers and elephants to live side by side. Farmers plant rows of chilli bushes around their fields, because elephants dislike the smell, and they hang beehives from the fence, since elephants are afraid of bees. The programme has reduced crop damage and given farmers an extra source of income from the honey. Dr Kamau believes that protecting elephants will succeed only if local people benefit, and that simple, cheap solutions are often better than expensive ones.
